name: Hot spring bathing

card.summary: Soaking in naturally heated mineral water (onsen) for relaxation, circulation and skin conditioning, which bathers associate with a smoother, fresher look.
card.note: Can aggravate high blood pressure or heart disease; poorly maintained baths have caused Legionella outbreaks.

quick.overview:
Hot spring bathing, best known as Japan's onsen tradition, is soaking in naturally heated, mineral-rich water. Bathers use it for relaxation and muscle relief, and many describe softer, smoother skin afterwards.

Its looks payoff runs through skin and wellbeing: warm mineral water, carbonated or acidic springs and relaxation are credited by promoters with skin conditioning. Studies exist for specific skin conditions and for blood pressure, but spa claims about beauty are described as promotional by encyclopedic sources.
quick.how: Bathers wash first, then soak nude in shared or private baths, indoor or outdoor; many skip the rinse afterwards to keep minerals on the skin. Water types include sulfur, sodium chloride, carbonated and iron springs.
quick.risks: Hot immersion can aggravate high blood pressure or heart disease, and reviews flag older adults and beta-blocker users. Poorly maintained baths have caused Legionella outbreaks, including one in 2002 that infected 295 people. Open wounds are usually a reason to stay out.

lead: Onsen are Japan's hot springs and the bathing facilities and inns around them; the country has about 25,000 spring sources and roughly 3,000 establishments using natural hot spring water [1]. Bathing there has a history of at least about 1,300 years [1].

Bathers associate mineral soaking with relaxation, circulation and skin condition; facilities advertise benefits such as smoother skin from carbonated water, though these are promotional and not firmly established [1]. The route to a better look is through skin conditioning and stress reduction rather than any structural change.
Research includes a controlled trial of acidic hot-spring bathing in 70 patients with refractory atopic dermatitis, and a review of blood-pressure responses to heat therapy [2][3].

angle.text: People use mineral baths to condition skin and unwind. The look benefit comes via skin feel and recovery, and varies by water type.

infobox: Wash first; no towels in water

paras: Onsen may be indoor or outdoor, and styles include steam, sand and waterfall baths [1]. Under Japan's Hot Springs Act, mineralized water must meet temperature and mineral criteria [1]. Etiquette calls for washing before entering, keeping towels out of the water and bathing nude; many people skip the post-bath shower to keep minerals on the skin [1].
Facilities advertise skin benefits by water type [1]. Grokipedia describes mineral-based skin conditioning and muscle relief but notes that validation varies by water type [4].

In a 1997 controlled study, 70 patients with refractory atopic dermatitis took 10-minute 42 degrees C acidic hot-spring baths twice daily; skin symptoms improved in 76% and skin Staphylococcus aureus fell in many responders [2].

A 2026 narrative review of heat therapy (saunas, hot spring bathing, hot water immersion, mudpack) found systolic blood pressure reductions of about 11-27 mmHg within 24 hours, but most studies lacked control groups, and safety in medicated and frail older adults remains unclear [3].

Onsen may aggravate high blood pressure or heart disease [1]. Legionella has been found in poorly maintained baths; a 2002 outbreak in Miyazaki infected 295 people and killed seven [1]. Many onsen advise people with open cuts to stay out and recommend keeping the head above water [1].
